item.title: NASA Outlines the Details of Artemis III and IV Missions
item.dc:creator: Douglas Gorman
item.description:

The post NASA Outlines the Details of Artemis III and IV Missions appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
NASA still wants to return US astronauts to the Moon in 2028. Today, officials shared a progress update on their efforts, as well as the finer details of the mission plans for Artemis III and IV, targeting flights in 2027 and 2028, respectively. 

Long story short: NASA remains confident it can meet the timeline for both missions. 

The agenda: For Artemis III, NASA is planning to fly a 14- to 17-day mission in LEO, testing three launch vehicles, one lunar lander, and the Orion crew capsule:

  • The mission will begin with an uncrewed launch of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket, carrying the company’s Blue Moon test lander.
  • NASA’s SLS rocket will launch the Artemis III crew and the Orion spacecraft to orbit “as soon as we can thereafter,” according to NASA Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons.
  • On Day 3, or once both spacecraft are in orbit, Orion and the Blue Moon test lander will attempt to rendezvous and dock.
  • On Days 4 and 5, the crew will enter Blue Moon to validate the lander’s subsystems—including tests of environmental controls, life-support systems, and emergency scenarios.
  • On Day 6, SpaceX’s Starship will launch to orbit.
  • On Day 8, Starship will attempt to rendezvous and dock with the crewed Orion vehicle. The Artemis III crew won’t transfer from Orion to Starship during this two-hour test, but officials didn’t share why. 
  • Following the Starship docking demo, the Artemis III crew will use the remaining days of the mission to complete additional tests on Orion, including tests of the new survival suit.

Above and beyond: For Artemis IV, NASA officials laid out two different mission plans—one using SpaceX’s Starship launcher and human landing system (HLS), and the other using Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket and Mark 2 lander.

While officials didn’t confirm which company would be selected for the historic lunar landing attempt, they said that both companies are making progress, and either or both could be ready in time for NASA’s end-of-2028 goal. 

There’s still a long road ahead for both companies, as Blue Origin has yet to return New Glenn to flight following its on-the-pad explosion in May, and SpaceX just notched its first uncrewed orbital flight with Starship in September. 

Even still, officials remained confident that both companies will have more than enough launches under their belt before the Artemis IV planning team gets antsy. 

“You will have multiple launches of Starship before we go conduct Artemis III, and you will have multiple launches of the Blue Origin New Glenn vehicle from the rebuilt pad before we go launch Artemis III, and so that’s going to give us a lot of confidence,” Parsons said.

Officials also confirmed that SpaceX will attempt to demonstrate its ability to transfer propulsion in orbit in early 2027, a key capability in the company’s plans to get its HLS to the lunar surface.

Zoom out: As he did at Payload’s Off World event last month, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman spent the bulk of his time at the lectern explaining why NASA wants to reach the Moon in two years: Once again, it’s all about beating China. 

Earlier this year, Isaacman predicted China would send a crewed mission around the moon in 2027, and that NASA ‘dodged a bullet’ when the uncrewed Chang’e-6 lander targeting the Moon’s south pole (near water resources both the China and US want) was delayed from this year. As such, he maintained the US should not relax its pace to reach the Moon.

“Here we are today, very much in a new space race, and despite decades of accumulated knowledge and extraordinary advancements in technology, this race will be much closer than it ever needed to be,” Isaacman said at the Friday update. “We will never launch until we are ready, but we will not accept that great achievements simply require more time and more money, nor will NASA sit idly by and watch one of the most consequential moments of this new century pass [to] our overseas competitors.”

Isaacman was upfront about the agency’s efforts to keep to its self-imposed timeline, and recently told the NASA workforce that Artemis III is, on paper, about 90 days behind schedule—but not for a lack of effort. 

Throughout the press conference, NASA officials gave countless examples of how the agency is working with vendors to accelerate supply chains, stretch hardware capabilities to do more (specifically, updates to create a “stretch” Vulcan rocket for Artemis III), and shrink requirements (i.e. on the Axiom spacesuit) to meet tighter deadlines for Artemis IV. 

“Every time we run into a supplier issue, a priority issue across the industry, Administrator Isaacman [and Associate Administrator] Amit [Kshatriya] are immediately on the phone. They’re immediately putting pressure. We’re immediately going out and helping to make things happen,” Parsons said.

The post NASA Outlines the Details of Artemis III and IV Missions appeared first on Payload.

item.title: Exclusive: DoD Taps Orbital Operations for Cryogenic Spacecraft Demo
item.dc:creator: Victoria Woodburn
item.description:
The Long Beach, CA, startup has won up to $35M from the DoD under a prototype Other Transaction Agreement to fly a full-scale, in-orbit demo of Astraeus—its cryogenic-maneuvering vehicle.

The post Exclusive: DoD Taps Orbital Operations for Cryogenic Spacecraft Demo appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, the Lockheed C-130 Hercules aircraft and variants have hauled cargo, flown as gunships, and refueled military jets midair. Now, Orbital Operations wants to do the same in space.

The Long Beach, CA, startup has won up to $35M from the DoD under a prototype Other Transaction Agreement to fly a full-scale, in-orbit demo of Astraeus—its cryogenic-maneuvering vehicle.

The company also closed a $7M seed extension led by DTX Ventures, bringing its total raised to ~$16M. GoAhead Ventures and Solaris Ventures also participated alongside follow-on investment from Initialized Capital, Harpoon Ventures, TRAC VC, and others. 

“Space is now a contested environment,” Orbital Operations CEO and cofounder Ben Schleuniger told Payload. “We’re going into this new space age where there’s all these new orbits and all of these new ideas coming around…we just need more dynamic assets out there to transport things around.” 

Meet Astraeus: The vehicle is designed to bring launch-vehicle-class propulsion to on-orbit operations. 

  • An onboard refrigeration system is designed to keep Astraeus’ liquid hydrogen and oxygen from boiling off, with the goal of keeping the vehicle on-orbit for years—much longer than the week or so that a disposable stage lasts.
  • The company is aiming to be able to carry out maneuvers within single-digit hours of giving a command, well inside the 48-hour window Schleuniger said military operators want.
  • After ferrying payloads to higher orbits, Astraeus is built to return to LEO to refuel.
  • The same base vehicle can be fitted for logistics, tactical, or refueling missions, mirroring the C-130’s mission-dependent variants.

“In a sense, we’re looking to be that reusable third stage,” Schleuniger said, adding, “It’s very dual use, but it also unlocks just all dynamic operations out in orbit—not just range, but speed.”

Cosmic timing: Schleuniger didn’t have to look far for an example of why the Pentagon wants these capabilities. Over the past week, Russia’s Cosmos 2612 shadowed ICEYE-X36, a US-flagged radar sat widely believed to supply imagery to Ukraine. LeoLabs tracked the Russian spacecraft closing to ~500 m between Oct. 15 and 19, before it drifted away. 

Still, Schleuniger said demand was already high “even before we had the incident this last week.” He pointed to SPACECOM’s list of tech priorities for 2029 to 2033, which names sustained space maneuver as one of its top needs. 

Later stage: The ~13-person team went from closing its seed round to a full-pressure hot-fire in under six months. Next up are more engine hot-fires, refrigeration-cycle work, and qualification before flight.

More fundraising is likely, but the government award “is really to get us to that first flight,” Schleuniger said. 

The post Exclusive: DoD Taps Orbital Operations for Cryogenic Spacecraft Demo appeared first on Payload.

item.title: Inside Starburst’s First Flight, and Portal’s New Bothell Office
item.dc:creator: Jacqueline Feldscher
item.description:
“I feel like 80% success now,” CEO Jeff Thurnburg said. “But honestly, to get this far this fast, I’m tempted to call it 100%.”

The post Inside Starburst’s First Flight, and Portal’s New Bothell Office appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
BOTHELL, WA—Portal Space Systems’ Starburst-1 spacecraft has been in orbit for just a couple days, and CEO Jeff Thornburg is already ready to declare the mission a success.

The spacecraft launched on Tuesday aboard SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 rideshare mission. After launch, Starburst separated from the rocket, began communicating with the ground, and unfurled its solar arrays to charge up its batteries. That’s the moment Thornburg said he and the 60+ person Portal team could relax—at least a little bit. 

“The relief came in stages,” he said. “The last big one came a couple hours after [launch] when we found the spacecraft. It was where we thought it was, it was communicating, and then it was like, ‘Oh my gosh, this has happened.’”

Second act: Thornburg is proud of what the team has accomplished so far on Starburst’s first flight, noting that many inaugural spacecraft fail due to power issues, communications troubles, or even just an inability to locate the satellite after separation. But Starburst’s mission is far from over.

Thornburg said the spacecraft is expected to fire up its thrusters for the first time “over the next few days,” and the team will take Starburst through a series of propulsive maneuvers. 

“I feel like 80% success now,” he said. “I call it a success right now mainly because we made it through launch, we made it through early checkouts…and we have complete control and confidence in the system right now. The other 20% is going to come with the activation of our ammonia-propulsion system, and when we do that, I’m going to call it 100% mission success. But honestly, to get this far this fast, I’m tempted to call it 100% mission success now.” 

Customers aren’t waiting for the mission to be declared a full success. Thornburg said three prospective commercial customers in the final stages of negotiations for Starburst are encouraged by the mission so far—and that a flood of demand has poured in over the past 48 hours since the launch.

Ride along: Thornburg acknowledged that full success also means Portal’s customers have a positive mission outcome. Starburst-1 has three payloads:

  • An attitude-control system from Zenno Astronautics to help orient the spacecraft using Earth’s magnetic field.
  • A camera from TRL11 to provide live video of the spacecraft, plus edge processing capabilities.
  • Atomic-6’s Space Armor tiles, to protect the spacecraft from debris impacts.

It’s the first spaceflight for the Space Armor. But Atomic-6 CEO Trevor Smith said the company won’t know how well the armor performed until it gets hit with debris, which can be captured by the on-board camera. 

“We’re crossing our fingers hoping to get hit,” Smith said. “If we can get the impact on camera and check the telemetry, we can say it worked in the operational environment.”

Holy ground: The Starburst that’s in orbit was built in Portal’s previous 6,000-sq.-ft. facility. The future fleet will be built in the company’s new 65,000-sq.-ft. manufacturing space that opened in August.

While Portal will use the space to build hardware that will reach for the heavens, the building has a history of searching for heaven in a different way—as a former mega-church.

Remnants of the building’s previous life remain. Thornburg shows me a mostly empty room that will host future avionics and flight software testing on flat sats. On the wall, kids’ drawings are still tacked up, with colorful scribbles that say “Jesus is coming back soon” and “the Lord is my shepherd.” 

The new facility will be designed to pump out 28 spacecraft a year—16 Starbursts, and 12 Supernovas, Portal’s larger, more powerful maneuverable spacecraft. The facility also houses a mission control, where Portal’s team is actively tracking Starburst in orbit—the line of slippers by the door a tangible reminder of the long overnight shifts the team has been pulling after the launch.

The modern building, parts of which are still under construction, is still a work in progress. Thornburg lays out his vision for the path spacecraft will take across the manufacturing floor—now bare—including in-house testing capability by the back wall, and a clean room for customer integration. 

In a nod to employee comfort, there are lots of windows to let in natural light to fight off seasonal depression from the Pacific Northwest’s cloudy weather. While much of the hardware still needs to be moved to the new facility, the branding is there in full force, including a fresh coat of blue-painted letters denoting the various rooms—all with names themed around Star Trek. 

There’s the Captain’s Quarters (Thornburg’s office), Excelsior (a Starfleet starship) and Galileo (a shuttlecraft assigned to the USS Enterprise). But my favorite room is the Holodeck, a nod to the Star Trek facility that can become anything. The multipurpose room will host social gatherings and all-hands meetings, Thornburg tells me. But it’s built for more than just the employees.

Near the entrance is a large orange wrap around tube slide—the kind you’d find at a playground, or McDonald’s PlayPlace. It’s a relic of the mega-church’s nursery that Thornburg said he told construction crews to leave to be used by young-at-heart employees—and the actual children of those building Portal’s spacecraft. 

“They may not know what their parents do, but they know that mom or dad has a cool slide at work,” Thornburg said.

The post Inside Starburst’s First Flight, and Portal’s New Bothell Office appeared first on Payload.

item.title: European MNOs Join Forces to Explore Joint MSS Spectrum Bid
item.dc:creator: Douglas Gorman
item.description:
Deutsche Telekom, Telefónica, Orange, and Vodafone plan to establish ground network infrastructure across Europe, and partner with an as-yet undetermined satellite operator for the D2D connection.

The post European MNOs Join Forces to Explore Joint MSS Spectrum Bid appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
Four major European mobile network operators (MNOs) are joining forces to explore a potential bid for future allocation of mobile satellite service (MSS) spectrum, as part of a strategy to provide the European market with D2D services.

Under the letter of intent, signed this week, Deutsche Telekom, Telefónica, Orange, and Vodafone plan to establish ground network infrastructure across Europe, and partner with an as-yet undetermined satellite operator for the D2D connection.

The deets: The news comes nearly six months after the European Commission proposed a new process for doling out licenses for 2 GHz frequency spectrum—the ideal band for D2D—which would set aside the majority of the total frequency rights to European operators:

  • One-third of the 2 GHz MSS band spectrum would be dedicated to government use for critical comms, security, and military applications—and must be provided by an EU operator.
  • One-third of the rights would only be available to EU operators for commercial uses, specifically applications like D2D and IoT.
  • The final third is open to any satellite operators—EU and non-EU alike.

At a time when competition for spectrum rights are spurring multi-billion-dollar deals, the proposed legislation opens the door for the four-way MNO partnership to access a walled-off portion of spectrum for a European-led D2D service.

It’s not immediately clear which bucket of spectrum rights the four-way MNO partnership is going to bid on, but the wording of the announcement suggests that it could focus on both the security and commercial layers.

“The joint initiative…has a clear ambition: To meet customer demand for universal coverage in underserved areas, strengthen the resilience of public networks, protect critical communications, and support the development of a European constellation,” the release states.

All for one: While the partnership stands to streamline access to D2D services for the four MNOs themselves, a successful bid for MSS spectrum could open the door for MNOs across the region to access the new capability.

“These services would be offered through a model designed to foster competition, reduce market fragmentation, and expand consumer choice across Europe,” the release said.

It’s still early days for D2D connectivity—the first European D2D message was sent just last year—and there’s no shortage of doubt over whether the new capability has a viable market in Europe. For instance, at World Space Business Week in Paris this September, Orange’s SVP of international infrastructure, Stéphane Cugnon de Sévricourt, questioned the size of the market for D2D in Europe—given that 98%+ of the region is already covered by terrestrial networks.

For Deutsche Telekom, the opportunity in D2D lies in the combination of satcom and terrestrial capabilities.

“We see satellite communications as a complementary technology and an important addition to our networks. They can extend coverage, but they cannot replace the capacity, stability, low latency, indoor coverage and reliability of terrestrial networks,” a spokesperson for Deutsche Telekom told Payload via email. “Satellites can extend coverage, while fiber and mobile networks provide the capacity, quality and scalability needed to support these applications.”

Orange and Vodafone declined to comment on the LOI, and Telefónica did not respond to Payload’s request for more details.

The Starlink in the room: The MNO partnership comes at a time when Europe is attempting to wean itself off of its reliance on international partners for satcom connectivity. But that effort is easier said than done.

To date, the lack of available European alternatives in D2D has forced some MNOs—including Deutsche Telekom and Telefónica—to partner with SpaceX Starlink. So, the big, unanswered question remains: Will the new four-way partnership double down on this international reliance—by selecting a foreign satellite operator as its D2D partner—or attempt to back a European-led alternative?

For some outside observers, the partnership is being viewed with “cautious positivity,” ESPI Research Fellow Elisabeth Clemmons told Payload via email. 

“The joint venture is European in nature, and of course is aimed at advancing Europe-wide D2D connectivity. But we view this as fulfilling only one of the two core objectives set out in the EC’s recitals,” Clemmons said. “Specifically, it contributes to the ‘provision of mobile satellite services’ in this band, but it does not necessarily ensure actual ‘development of a satellite project’ as described in the regulation proposal.”

The post European MNOs Join Forces to Explore Joint MSS Spectrum Bid appeared first on Payload.

item.title: Xona Raises $250M Series D to Scale Commercial GPS Constellation
item.dc:creator: Douglas Gorman
item.description:
Xona’s long-term plan is to build a ~258-sat constellation to offer an upgraded commercial alternative to government GPS networks.

The post Xona Raises $250M Series D to Scale Commercial GPS Constellation appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
Xona Space Systems announced a $250M Series D today to accelerate production of its Pulsar commercial GPS constellation, which is aiming to begin service in 2027.

Steve Jurvetson, cofounder and managing director of Future Ventures, led the round, which included additional participation from undisclosed new and existing investors. The round, which valued the company at $2.45B, brings Xona’s fundraising to $570M+ since its founding in 2019.

Location, location, location: Xona’s long-term plan is to build a ~258-sat constellation to offer an upgraded commercial alternative to government GPS networks. Xona’s pitch: GPS is a critical capability underpinning much of the modern economy, but publicly funded GPS networks are costly, complex, and too exposed to spoofing and jamming.

Xona’s alternative, Pulsar, aims to offer centimeter-level precision, jamming resistance, and the ability to reach receivers indoors—with signals that are 100x more powerful than legacy GPS.

In August, Xona became the first commercial GPS constellation to win FCC approval to broadcast L-band signals. Next year, the company plans to test its integrations with Army, Navy, and Air Force assets. For the military, the timing couldn’t be better.

Xona has seen an uptick in interest from government customers “coming on the heels of increased jamming and spoofing vulnerability seen from places like the Strait of Hormuz, where interference has disrupted navigation for more than 2,000 ships,” CEO Brian Manning told Payload via email.

And demand is coming from all sides, Manning said.

“On the commercial side, we’re seeing strong demand signals across all types of innovations in autonomous vehicles and robotics, aviation, and critical infrastructure,” he said. “We’re on track to begin serving early commercial users with a timing service next year.”

Output volume: The announcement comes days after Xona received $15M CDN (~$10.7M) from Canada to expand operations in Montreal, QC, and launched six Pulsar satellites to orbit on SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 rideshare launch. The sats include four modified Pulsar-0 sats, built with help from Aerospacelab, and two Pulsar Test Satellites designed and manufactured by Xona in-house.

The launch represents the first stage of Pulsar’s full commercial PNT constellation—with the four Aerospacelab-built sats beginning the service, and the two Pulsar Test Satellites validating the in-house design before the company scales to full production.

Xona plans to use the new capital to catalyze its output, and has spent much of 2026 laying the groundwork for a capacity boom. In April, the company opened a new production facility in Burlingame, CA, and this month announced the hiring of Waymo veteran Patrick Cadariu as COO to lead the production increase.

“We’re moving from development into repeatable satellite production, with a goal of reaching capacity to produce 50 satellites annually by the end of 2027,” Manning said.

The post Xona Raises $250M Series D to Scale Commercial GPS Constellation appeared first on Payload.

item.title: National Academies Rank Nonpolar Moon Sites
item.dc:creator: Victoria Woodburn
item.description:
A new report from the National Academies ranks the top four non-polar sites for future crewed lunar missions.

The post National Academies Rank Nonpolar Moon Sites appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
Location, location, location is everything—even on the Moon. 

Astronauts are heading back to the lunar surface, and now the scientific community has made its voice heard on where they should go with the release yesterday of a National Academies report ranking the top four non-polar sites for future crewed lunar missions.

NASA asked the committee which science goals in locations beyond the poles need people rather than robots, and where to send those astronauts. The committee’s answer assumes short sorties: two-person crews, no rover, and one to four moonwalks per site.

Sites were weighed on three criteria: whether science aligned with the decadal surveys and NASA’s Moon to Mars objectives, if the missions would expand US exploration capabilities, and, to a lesser degree, how they would contribute to public inspiration.

Site seeing: The sites, in priority order:

  • Bhabha Crater: Astronauts have never landed this far from Earth. The far-side crater sits in the middle of the South Pole-Aitken Basin, which may have the oldest impact signature in the solar system. The region is also shielded from Earth’s radio noise, making it a prime spot for low-frequency astronomy.
  • Mons Hadley: Apollo 11 and 17 are seen by NASA as protected heritage sites because of their historical significance, so the committee picked the Apollo 15 site instead. Crews would land ~2 km away from the Apollo site and venture over to investigate how the hardware and astronaut waste left behind have held up after 55+ years.
  • Orientale Basin: It’s the Moon’s youngest large impact basin—and best-preserved. Boulders that tumbled off the region’s inner mountain rings could give scientists their first look at the deep lunar crust. The committee suggests only a single visit, keeping the site undisturbed for a gravitational wave observatory.
  • Aristarchus Plateau: The volcanic plateau was a planned Apollo landing site and may hold water-bearing deposits and rare Earth elements. It’s also a good spot for a space-weather observatory.

Off the beaten path: NASA commissioned the study in 2025, before the agency refocused its lunar program on a Moon Base on the lunar South Pole. With the shifts, the committee is now pitching the sorties as add-ons to the Moon Base missions. NASA has not said whether it will act on the recommendations.

The list may also have a nearer-term use. If schedule or other constraints keep Artemis IV away from the absolute South Pole, Interstellar Mapping CEO Andrew Hazelton told Payload, sites farther from it “could meet many of the same objectives with potentially lower landing risk.”

For companies like his, he added, “every new data point helps, and the sites in this report would add several.”

Packing list: The committee left the how to NASA, but provided the agency with a suggestion list:

  • Let astronauts roam beyond NASA’s current 2-km limit on how far astronauts can travel from the lander, ideally on an unpressurized rover.
  • Develop survive-the-night instruments, continue high-resolution orbital reconnaissance, and maintain continuous comms during surface ops.
  • Run the same baseline experiments at every location, like crew health monitoring and seismic stations for a Lunar Geophysical Network.
  • Pay for the labs and scientists who will actually study the samples.

The post National Academies Rank Nonpolar Moon Sites appeared first on Payload.

item.title: Hewlett Packard Enterprise to Send AI Compute Module to the Moon
item.dc:creator: Douglas Gorman
item.description:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise ($HPE) is taking remote working to a whole new level.

The post Hewlett Packard Enterprise to Send AI Compute Module to the Moon appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise ($HPE) is taking remote working to a whole new level.

HPE announced that its new AI-compute module—dubbed Spaceborne Computer-4—is set to deploy on Astrolab’s FLIP rover during a mission expected to launch this year.

Bit FLIP: During the mission, HPE’s Spaceborne Computer-4 will test large language models, visual and LiDAR data processing, as well as autonomous monitoring on the lunar surface. NASA and Deloitte also plan to deploy AI workloads on Computer-4.

  • NASA will run a neural-net model trained on Earth, Moon, and ISS data to demonstrate the coordination of multiple, separate AI models.
  • Deloitte will deploy its Silent Shield system to detect cyber intrusions, and provide near-real-time analytics and spot anomalies.

HPE will also support the mission on the backend, deploying its software at Astrolab’s mission control to optimize the delivery of insights and manage the automated workloads.

The goal is to lay the groundwork for future Moon excursions to leverage edge computing to do more during lunar sojourns—including utilizing in-situ data to map the lunar surface, and demonstrating reliable, scalable deployment of future AI applications.

“What’s exciting is giving the rover the ability to make sense of what it collects, rather than simply sending everything home for analysis,” Mark Fernandez, HPE’s chief scientist of space technologies and solutions, told Payload via email. “For Astrolab, NASA and Deloitte, that’s an opportunity to test how onboard computing could deliver useful insights faster and make better use of communications with Earth.”

Fourth times the charm: As the name suggests, Spaceborne Computer-4 isn’t HPE’s first foray into space-based computing. Computer-4 stands on the shoulders of three earlier models that flew to the ISS in 2017, 2021, and 2024. These missions first tested whether COTS parts could work in space, and then demonstrated successive upgrades to compute power and storage, as well as the ability to run onboard AI.

However, Computer-4 is HPE’s first Spaceborne Computer to operate in the vacuum of space.

  • Computer-4 is equipped with a low-power CPU and GPU, and utilizes flash-memory storage inside solid-state drives from KIOXIA.
  • The system is designed to weather the lunar environment by operating without fans, instead using a space radiator to keep the system from overheating. 
  • Computer-4 is also engineered to monitor the effects of radiation, and lower its compute power during episodes that could damage the hardware.

The post Hewlett Packard Enterprise to Send AI Compute Module to the Moon appeared first on Payload.

item.title: SpaceX’s AI Revenue Leads Q3 Earnings
item.dc:creator: Victoria Woodburn
item.description:
With its first full quarter as a public company under its belt, SpaceX blew past expectations Tuesday with ~$14.6B in revenue and net income of $4.4B.

The post SpaceX’s AI Revenue Leads Q3 Earnings appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
With its first full quarter as a public company under its belt, SpaceX blew past expectations Tuesday with ~$14.7B in revenue and net income of $4.4B. 

The revenue number is up 87% from Q2 and 161% YoY—plus substantially higher than the ~$12.8B that analysts had expected.

Once again, SpaceX’s earnings are as much an AI story as a space one. The Evel Knievel–esque (or Hot Rod, for the millennials) unveiling of a flying Tesla Roadster last week added fuel to the Tesla-SpaceX merger rumors. But the bigger surprise was in the numbers. For the first time, SpaceX’s AI business, rebranded as SpaceXSI for “Super Intelligence,” out-earned Starlink.

So let’s take a peek under the hood.

Rent’s due: Space revenue in Q3 jumped 84% compared to the previous quarter to $1.8B despite fewer launches—35, compared with 38 in Q2—as more of them carried paying customers. 

  • The segment lost just $7M, nearly breaking even after a $542M loss in Q2. That’s despite spending $1.2B on R&D, mostly for Starship.
  • SpaceX flew 12 customer launches, up from 10 in Q2.
  • The company dubbed Flight 14—SpaceX’s first orbital Starship flight—its first revenue-generating Starship mission.

SpaceX will try to catch both the booster and the ship next month on Flight 15. During the earnings call, Elon Musk called success “more likely than not” and said he expects weekly Starship flights in the first half of 2027.

Middle child: Starlink is still SpaceX’s biggest profit-maker, earning $2.4B in operating income on $5.2B in revenue. That revenue now makes up 36% of the company’s total, down from 55% in Q2, as AI pulled ahead.

  • SpaceX added 1.6M consumer subscribers, bringing the total to 13.6M. That count no longer includes managed enterprise and government accounts, such as airlines and ships.
  • The average subscriber paid $69 a month, up from $66, as more growth came from developed markets where plans cost more.
  • Enterprise and government revenue nearly doubled from a year ago, to $2.1B.
  • Starlink Mobile now has 22M monthly users, up 37% since Q2.

Main character energy: SpaceXSI brought in $7.6B in Q3, nearly triple its Q2 total and more than half of SpaceX’s revenue. Cloud deals accounted for most of the jump, with Cursor and Grok adding the rest.

  • SpaceXSI turned a profit, earning $431M in operating income after losing $1.3B in Q2.
  • It also makes up the bulk of spending, accounting for $16.4B of SpaceX’s $19.6B in Q3 capex.
  • Cursor—acquired in August—has already brought in $608M.

Johnsen said new compute pays for itself in less than a year, and Musk said SpaceX could rent out its compute “several times over.” For now, SpaceX is keeping contracts short so it can charge more at renewal.

SpaceX had 1.7 GW of compute at the end of Q3 and expects 2.5 GW to 3 GW by December. Musk said he’s “highly confident” the business can add another 10 GW next year.

One more thing: SpaceX still spends more cash than it brings in, and Q4 will cost even more. The company projected capex will balloon to $35B to $40B, roughly double Q3 spend.

Management anticipates that the spending will pay off fast, forecasting $33B to $37B in revenue for Q1 2027. Musk took estimates a step further, putting annualized revenue at $500B to $1T by the end of 2027.

As for the rumored Tesla merger, Musk said calling it a done deal “would be overstating it.” The two companies haven’t agreed on terms, and shareholders would still need to vote.

The post SpaceX’s AI Revenue Leads Q3 Earnings appeared first on Payload.

item.title: Congress Seeks Answers On Starlink Disruptions in Ukraine
item.dc:creator: Jacqueline Feldscher
item.description:
“The United States government has a fundamental obligation to protect American personnel serving overseas,” the senators wrote. “The possibility that American personnel were endangered by preventable disruptions, inadequate coordination, or decisions made by their own government demands immediate scrutiny and accountability.”

The post Congress Seeks Answers On Starlink Disruptions in Ukraine appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
Senators are demanding answers about what caused the disruptions to SpaceX Starlink connectivity in Ukraine—and what consequences the comms outage had. 

Starlink terminals supporting Ukrainian operations reportedly had speed restrictions imposed between Oct. 12 and 14. The limitations impacted Ukrainian drone and aircraft operations, potentially impacting the military’s response to Russian drone and missile attacks, according to the senators, who also raised concerns about “glitches” that affected intelligence sharing and early missile warning.

The buck stops…where?: Four Democratic senators sent a letter to SpaceX on Monday demanding that the company explain what role, if any, it had in the outages. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that any changes to Starshield—a military version of Starlink developed for the government—were the result of decisions made by the US government. 

The letter to Christopher Cardaci, VP of legal at SpaceX, is searching for answers to questions including:

  • What restrictions were put enacted during the three day time period this month;
  • Who made or was notified about those decisions;
  • More broadly, who has the power to revoke or restrike Starlink access in Ukraine. 

Grave concerns: A bipartisan group of nine senators also sent a letter to the Pentagon’s inspector general on Thursday, expressing “grave concern” over the Starlink disruptions in Ukraine—including reports that American personnel could not reach safety during attacks because of the comms breakdown. The senators also called for Ukrainian military operations to receive the unlimited Starlink speeds that were originally promised.

Specifically, the senators are asking the IG to determine:

  • If the disruptions impacted whether American personnel were able to shelter amid the Russian attacks;
  • If the US government knew about or approved the reported slowdowns, and whether they were driven by SpaceX;
  • What caused the speed restrictions—including policy decisions, or technical problems;
  • What DoD is doing to make sure Americans remain safe—and receive adequate missile-warning info going forward.

“The United States government has a fundamental obligation to protect American personnel serving overseas,” the senators wrote. “The possibility that American personnel were endangered by preventable disruptions, inadequate coordination, or decisions made by their own government demands immediate scrutiny and accountability.”

The concern is bicameral—Rep. Mike Turner (R-OH) on Sunday called for Congress to investigate the outages.

Around the world: Starlink is making policy headlines around the world, not just in Ukraine.

  • SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that Starlink was being blocked from beginning service in India by Reliance Industries Chair and Managing Director Mukesh Ambani, in an attempt to squelch competition. The company has fired back, saying that it has “never feared competition,” while its own satellite internet constellation awaits government approval.
  • The EU has also threatened to limit access to spectrum for non-European companies, including SpaceX, provoking promises of “devastating” retaliation from Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU. 

The post Congress Seeks Answers On Starlink Disruptions in Ukraine appeared first on Payload.

item.title: State Department Taps Trio for $5M Space Diplomacy Push
item.dc:creator: Victoria Woodburn
item.description:
At last week’s second annual US Space Forum, the US Mission to the International Organizations in Vienna launched Project Constellation, a $5M effort to build international space partnerships.

The post State Department Taps Trio for $5M Space Diplomacy Push appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
The State Department is starstruck.  

At last week’s second annual US Space Forum, the US Mission to the International Organizations in Vienna launched Project Constellation, a $5M effort to build international space partnerships.

During the next two years, the program will run talent exchanges, delegation visits, and training with the aim of connecting emerging space nations with US companies. Per the State Department, it’s also meant to drive closer alignment of foreign governments’ civil and commercial space positions at the UN’s Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and General Assembly.

“Today’s aspiring, emerging, and developing space nations will be tomorrow’s satellite constellation operators,” Wells Griffith, the ambassador of the US Mission to International Organizations in Vienna, said in remarks announcing the program.

Starring: The State Department tapped three US organizations to run the program:

  • Meridian International Center—the prime recipient—will oversee strategy, delivery, partner coordination, and finances, and organize exchanges through its diplomatic and industry networks.
  • The Commercial Space Federation will lead the commercial side, promoting procurement and building business partnerships with US companies.
  • SPACEAIMS—a public policy consulting firm—will guide the law, policy, governance, and diplomacy work, including country assessments, policy dialogues, and training.

Kelli Kedis Ogborn, strategic advisor at CSF, told Payload via email that US companies are “already delivering capabilities and building cross-border relationships that turn cooperation into practice.”

First light: The program’s first task? Make sure people know it exists. Early-awareness efforts will target US foreign service officers and the US embassy community.

Also on the docket are the 2027 and 2028 US Space Forums, plus trips in which international leaders visit the US and American commercial space leaders go to emerging space nations. The net is wide—more than 70 countries across the globe—though country-specific plans will be developed with partners. Griffith also teased a partnership-pitch competition, innovation showcases, and investor engagement.

Binary system: Project Constellation is State’s second space-diplomacy push in as many months. In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio unveiled the Space Catalyst Partnership (SCP) to deepen cooperation with Artemis Accords signatories, starting with $6.5M awarded over two years aiming for satellite internet in rural southern Peru.

The two efforts orbit different centers of gravity. SCP is members-only—Accords signatories can join, and foreign aid helps them buy American. Constellation plays to the whole room in Vienna, pitching US policy as a helpful template for other nations.

The post State Department Taps Trio for $5M Space Diplomacy Push appeared first on Payload.

item.title: Reaction Dynamics Targets 2031 for Borealis Medium-Lift Launch
item.dc:creator: Douglas Gorman
item.description:
In the contest to build up commercial launch capabilities in Canada, Quebec-based startup Reaction Dynamics has entered a new weight class.

The post Reaction Dynamics Targets 2031 for Borealis Medium-Lift Launch appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
In the contest to build up commercial launch capabilities in Canada, Quebec-based startup Reaction Dynamics has entered a new weight class.

The launcher today unveiled its medium-lift rocket—called Borealis—which is targeting a debut orbital launch attempt in 2031.

Borealis’ 6,000 kg to LEO payload capacity represents a massive leap compared with the company’s ~200 kg capacity Aurora small-lift launcher—which is targeting a first orbital launch attempt in Q4 2028. But both vehicles are built on much of the same underlying technology.

State matters: For the bulk of Reaction Dynamics’ ~10-year history, the company has been developing a hybrid rocket engine reliant on a mix of solid fuel and liquid oxidizer, as part of a strategy to build a storable, deployable launch capability. However, the company pivoted last year to an entirely liquid-fueled alternative to accelerate the transition to heavier-lift launch vehicles. 

“The whole decision to transition Aurora to liquid is to be able to optimize for Borealis,” Jesse Mikelberg, Reaction Dynamics’ director of business development and strategy, told Payload. “Instead of having two separate vehicle programs, two separate propulsion programs, one based on a solid fuel, one based on a liquid fuel… we are still in the process of transitioning Aurora to a development path that accelerates Borealis.”

Mikelberg explained that the transition to liquid fuel was the direct result of Canada’s increasing appetite for heavier-lift sovereign-launch capabilities. And at a time when SpaceX has signaled its intent to sunset the Transporter rideshare program, Reaction Dynamics is attempting to win some of the launch demand left in Transporter’s wake, and build a sovereign option for Canada that offers lift comparable with vehicles south-of-the-border. 

Since shifting to liquid across its vehicle portfolio—within the past year, according to Mikelberg—Reaction Dynamics has completed 21 hot-fire tests of the liquid-fueled engine. The Aurora development campaign will attempt to prove out some of the hardware planned for Borealis, including the avionics, tanks, and, eventually, an upgraded heavier-lift engine. 

Dollars and sense: To get Borealis to orbit, however, Reaction Dynamics is going to need a little more than engine tests. The company has raised ~$50M CDN ($35.4M), and is raising another $70M+ CDN ($49.9M+) Series B to fund the first launch of Aurora, and invest in a manufacturing capacity to churn out eight Auroras annually. 

Beyond Aurora, Mikelberg estimated the company would need an additional $200M+ CDN ($141.8M+) to support the transition to Borealis.

Altogether, the new capital will support the company’s plans to up its headcount fivefold—from 68 to 350+ by 2031—and fund a new 375,000 sq. ft. manufacturing and integration facility in Quebec that can produce 24 annual Borealis rockets.

Correction: This article was updated to correct a typo with the conversion rate from CDN to USD.

The post Reaction Dynamics Targets 2031 for Borealis Medium-Lift Launch appeared first on Payload.

item.title: Exclusive: EraDrive Lands $13M DoD Award For Autonomy Module
item.dc:creator: Douglas Gorman
item.description:
EraDrive won a $13M DoD award, under which the Space Force will buy an undisclosed number of the company’s Era-Node vision-based autonomy modules.

The post Exclusive: EraDrive Lands $13M DoD Award For Autonomy Module appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
EraDrive, the Palo Alto, CA-based startup building autonomous capabilities for satellites, won a $13M DoD award, under which the Space Force will buy an undisclosed number of the company’s Era-Node vision-based autonomy modules.

The Accelerate the Procurement and Fielding of Innovative Technologies (APFIT) award is intended to provide direct procurement funding for new capabilities, unlike R&D-focused awards such as SBIR and STTR. EraDrive’s award creates an accelerated pathway for the Space Force to acquire Era-Nodes for future spacecraft.

“Getting a small company’s technology onto a government contract usually takes years. Working with the APFIT office and NASA Ames, we got EraDrive selected and on contract within the same fiscal year. That’s the pace we need to keep up with what the commercial sector is building,” Lawrence Robertson, the Air Force’s lead for space experiments, told Payload via email.

Keys to the castle: Autonomous capabilities for military sats have been on the DoD’s wish list for years. While serving as the Space Force’s top acquisition official in 2024, Frank Calvelli said autonomous sats would be vital to helping the DoD get around downlink bottlenecks. But EraDrive officials claim that its tech provides a range of capabilities beyond just flying in GPS-denied environments.

“The way we think about GPS-denied navigation, space domain awareness, RPO, and autonomous operations is basically these are just like four different flavors of autonomy, which are just backed by the same stack,” EraDrive CEO Sumant Sharma told Payload.

EraDrive isn’t the only company building autonomous capabilities for satellite operations. But Sharma told Payload that he believes that many offerings in the market fall short of true autonomy.

  • Many autonomous operations work by uplinking a list of commands the satellite can perform between ground-links.
  • Era-Nodes, however, give more control to the satellite—where the operator can define an envelope of do’s-and-don’ts, which satellites are free to operate within.

Ducks flock together: While EraDrive has yet to fly its fully integrated Era-Node module in orbit, nearly all of the components and software onboard have notched flight heritage.

Over the past two years, EraDrive has flown at least seven experiments of its autonomous software—called Era-Core—onboard NASA’s Starling satellites, demonstrating that it can identify and track moving targets, and autonomously cue other sats to adjust themselves to keep space objects in view.

Going forward, EraDrive hopes each Era-Node in orbit can become part of a sensor network, “giving operators fleet-level intelligence for collision avoidance and SDA whether or not they fly our hardware,” Sharma told Payload via email.

The post Exclusive: EraDrive Lands $13M DoD Award For Autonomy Module appeared first on Payload.

item.title: WarpWare Closes Pre-Seed to Bring Agentic Tools to Flight Software
item.dc:creator: Victoria Woodburn
item.description:
CO-based WarpWare closed its $1.2M pre-seed round today to expand what it calls an AI-enabled engineering platform for space missions.

The post WarpWare Closes Pre-Seed to Bring Agentic Tools to Flight Software appeared first on Payload.
item.content:encoded:
For spacecraft software teams, every new program can feel like Groundhog Day.

CO-based WarpWare closed its $1.2M pre-seed round today to expand what it calls an AI-enabled engineering platform for space missions.

The round—raised through SAFEs—was primarily angel-funded. Angel groups including the Rockies Venture Club, Cowtown Angels, and the Aggie Angel Network joined individual angels and two space-focused early-stage funds, Vesper Alpha and Marlboro Lane Ventures. 

“Roughly 80% of the space software stack is expensive and time-consuming to build, but it is not proprietary,” WarpWare CEO and cofounder Alex Reynolds told Payload via email.

Origin story: WarpWare grew out of a question the founders had while working at Sierra Space: How much of the company’s flight software could be reused for a new vehicle? The answer—according to Reynolds and COO Mickey Mathew, also a cofounder—was almost none.

“Most teams are building many of the same foundational capabilities,” Reynolds said.  

  • Engineers often build flight software, guidance, navigation and control (GN&C), simulation and testing environments from scratch for each new program—dragging out timelines, raising costs, and adding technical risk, WarpWare officials say.
  • WarpWare replaces that ground-up approach with one connected platform covering flight software, GN&C, simulation, and testing.

WarpWare wants agentic workflows to take on more of that work, but the company says technical experts maintain control of mission-critical decisions. A space-specific AI harness ties into WarpWare’s tools and automatically runs multilayered testing on the outputs. Engineers decide where AI fits, where work stays fully human-led, and when an output is ready to move forward.

Building traction: WarpWare says its platform is used by 20+ organizations across a wide range of missions, including in-space power beaming, NASA science missions, cislunar missions, and launch vehicles.

  • LEAP flew the full platform on its Bullfrog rocket, which WarpWare says cut LEAP’s timeline to launch by 65%. 
  • WarpWare is also supporting Argotec on NASA’s MiniCOR space-weather mission, along with several startups preparing for first flights. 

The new funds will help bring agentic-engineering capabilities to more commercial and government space markets, WarpWare officials say, and build out sales and marketing to grow the company’s customer base.

The post WarpWare Closes Pre-Seed to Bring Agentic Tools to Flight Software appeared first on Payload.
